summary: Speaking on the glories of Sankirtan, Indradyumna Swami builds his talk on Jiva Goswami's Bhakti-sandarbha, which grades Krishna's moods across three abodes: Dwaraka (Krishna as king, the mood of awe and reverence), Mathura (his birthplace, more intimate), and Vrindavan (the gopis' pure, selfless, most perfect love), likening the difference to 9-karat versus 24-karat gold. He applies the same gradation to chanting the holy name: solitary japa is perfect, congregational temple kirtan is more perfect, but carrying the name to the people through street Sankirtan and book distribution (Brihat Mridanga) is most perfect, because the holy name is a person (nama cintamanih krsnah) who wants to go out and rescue the fallen souls who left the spiritual world. He stresses that chanting sixteen quality rounds daily is the foundation that gives a devotee the tejas (spiritual potency) to preach, since "people don't buy the book, they buy the book distributor," illustrating with stories of Prabhupada finishing his rounds in Los Angeles ("now I can do any damn thing I want"), a shy Latin American devotee who won book-distribution marathons in France simply by saying "Hare Bol" while shining like the sun, and a godbrother whose only qualification was that he "came running" to the maha-mantra. To show the auspiciousness that loud congregational chanting spreads, he recounts Krishna's headache being cured only by the dust of the gopis' feet and Chaitanya Bhagavata's account of dust from Mahaprabhu's kirtan party awakening ecstatic symptoms in distant farmers, adding that even the trees hearing kirtan are fortunate. Sankirtan devotees, he says, witness "little miracles" daily as strangers who came to forget God buy a book to remember him, and Krishna's promise "I am adventure" is realized on the street corner, which he calls the real temple where one meets God. Most of the lecture is a long autobiographical story from his book-distribution days in Paris: how he infiltrated locked fashion houses on the Champs-Elysees by picking locks and riding delivery trucks, tracked prospects with colored incense marks, and was eventually beaten by security guards, arrested, tied to a pole, and driven into a forest fearing he would be executed. The police chief then suddenly turned gentle, apologized, tended his wounds and fed him, revealing that a week earlier the swami had preached at his home, patiently listening to his life story for over an hour and reading the whole Bhagavad-gita with him chapter by chapter, comparing him to Arjuna, so that the former criminal came to believe in God and now read the Gita nightly with his family. Concluding that God had arranged the arrest so the two could meet again, Indradyumna Swami urges devotees to leave their comfort zone, depend on Krishna, and go out on Sankirtan, promising that this opportunity will remain available for ten thousand years.
key_points: Jiva Goswami's Bhakti-sandarbha grades the rasa of Krishna's three abodes: Dwaraka (aishvarya/awe), Mathura (growing intimacy), and Vrindavan (the gopis' most perfect madhurya love), compared to 9-, 18-, 22-, and 24-karat gold, with the gopis holding the 24-karat bhava.

The three ways of chanting parallel that gradation: japa is perfect, congregational temple kirtan is more perfect, and taking the name to the people via street Sankirtan and book distribution (Brihat Mridanga) is most perfect.

Sixteen quality rounds a day is the non-negotiable foundation of spiritual life and the source of the tejas that lets even a shy introvert preach, because "people don't buy the book, they buy the book distributor" (Rama also means spiritual strength; Krishna is the strength of the strong).
The holy name is a person, nondifferent from Krishna (nama cintamanih krsnah), who wants to go out and reclaim the fallen souls; facilitating that desire yields more mercy than one can hold.

Auspiciousness of loud congregational chanting shown through the pastime of Krishna's headache cured only by the dust of the gopis' feet, and Chaitanya Bhagavata's account of dust from Mahaprabhu's kirtan awakening the eight ecstatic symptoms in distant farmers; even nearby trees benefit.

Illustrative stories: Prabhupada's "now I can do any damn thing" after finishing his rounds; the Latin American devotee who won French marathons saying only "Hare Bol" while shining like the sun; the godbrother whose qualification was that he "came running" to the maha-mantra.

The central Paris story: infiltrating locked Champs-Elysees fashion houses by lock-picking and riding delivery trucks, color-coding prospects with incense ("in like a needle, out like a plow"), being beaten and subjected to a mock arrest/execution, only to discover the repentant police chief was a householder he had earlier converted with the Bhagavad-gita, the whole ordeal understood as Krishna's arrangement; the street corner is your temple where you meet God, and this chance lasts 10,000 years.
references: Bhakti-sandarbha (Jiva Goswami) — the gradation of devotional rasa across Dwaraka, Mathura, and Vrindavan that frames the entire talk.

Siksastakam verse 1 — "ceto-darpana-marjanam ... param vijayate sri-krsna-sankirtanam": congregational chanting cleanses the mirror of the heart (goodbye lust, anger, greed) and is the supreme victory; also quoted ("Param vijayate Sri Krishna Sankirtan") as the real victory won by preaching in the hardest places.

Siksastakam verse 8 — "aslisya va pada-ratam ... mat-prana-nathas tu sa eva naparah": the gopi's unconditional love — even if Krishna embraces her roughly or breaks her heart by not appearing, he remains her only worshipable Lord life after life.
Bhagavad-gita 7.11 — "balam balavatam caham": "I am the strength of the strong"; cited for the spiritual strength gained by chanting (with Rama also meaning spiritual strength).

Chaitanya-charitamrita, Madhya 17.133 (quoting Padma Purana) — "nama cintamanih krsnas caitanya-rasa-vigrahah ...": the holy name is Krishna himself, nondifferent from the named; basis for "the holy name is a person."
Brahma-samhita 5.29 — Vrindavan/the spiritual abode built of chintamani (transcendental touchstone); "Vrindavan is made of Chintamani."
Srimad Bhagavatam, Canto 10 (Krishna Book) — the pastime of curing Krishna's headache with the dust of the gopis' feet, Narada Muni searching the universe while other devotees fear the offense.

Chaitanya Bhagavata — the prediction that Krishna's name will be preached in every town and village ("prithivite ache yata nagaradi grama"), and the account of dust from Mahaprabhu's kirtan party (with Nityananda, Gadadhara, Advaita, Srivasa) awakening the eight ecstatic symptoms of love of God in distant farmers.

Bhagavad-gita — Krishna's statement that he is "adventure," realized by taking the chanting of Hare Krishna to the people in Kali-yuga (exact verse uncertain); the Ninth Chapter (Raja-vidya Raja-guhya) named as the converted police chief's favorite.
Nrsimha prayer — "namas te narasimhaya prahladahlada-dayine hiranyakasipor vaksah-sila-tanka-nakhalaye": sung by the swami while being beaten and arrested.
